claim: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the most common complication of diabetes mellitus defined as diabetes with albuminuria or an impaired glomerular filtration rate (GFR) or both.
source: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD; or diabetic nephropathy) is the most common complication of diabetes mellitus defined as diabetes with albuminuria or an impaired glomerular filtration rate (GFR) or both.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about DKD that draws from established medical knowledge and consensus.

claim: DKD is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease, necessitating dialysis or transplantation.
source: It is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease, necessitating dialysis or transplantation.
evidence: This statement reflects established clinical knowledge about DKD outcomes.

claim: The number of DKD patients continues to rise despite improved management of diabetes.
source: Despite improved management of diabetes, the number of DKD patients continues to rise, causing an enormous health and economic burden worldwide.
evidence: This is a general statement about epidemiological trends that draws from established knowledge.

claim: Classical histopathological features of DKD include glomerular changes such as podocyte hypertrophy and loss, glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules.
source: Classical histopathological features of DKD are glomerular changes such as podocyte hypertrophy and loss, glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules (Oshima et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oshima et al., 2021.

claim: Tubulointerstitial alterations, including peritubular fibrosis, contribute to or even drive DKD progression.
source: Often overlooked are the tubulointerstitial alterations, including peritubular fibrosis, that contribute to or even drive DKD progression (Bonventre, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bonventre, 2012.

claim: The recent success of sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors highlights the proximal tubule cell (PTC) as an important target in DKD therapy.
source: The recent success of sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors highlights the proximal tubule cell (PTC) as an important target in DKD therapy (DeFronzo et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DeFronzo et al., 2021.

claim: PTCs constitute more than half of renal mass.
source: Constituting more than half of renal mass (Park et al., 2018), PTCs reabsorb most of the solutes and proteins filtered by the glomerulus (Chevalier, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2018.

claim: PTCs reabsorb most of the solutes and proteins filtered by the glomerulus.
source: Constituting more than half of renal mass (Park et al., 2018), PTCs reabsorb most of the solutes and proteins filtered by the glomerulus (Chevalier, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chevalier, 2016.

claim: The energy for PTC tasks is almost exclusively provided by mitochondrial β-oxidation of fatty acids.
source: The energy for both tasks is almost exclusively provided by mitochondrial β-oxidation of fatty acids (Bobulescu, 2010; Kang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bobulescu, 2010 and Kang et al., 2015.

claim: In mice fed with a high-fat diet (HFD) or in individuals with type 2 diabetes, lipids accumulate predominantly in PTCs.
source: Accordingly, in mice fed with a high-fat diet (HFD) or in individuals with type 2 diabetes, lipids accumulate predominantly in PTCs (Herman-Edelstein et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2015; Rampanelli et al., 2018), indicating that these cells may be equipped with a high capacity to take up and store lipids.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Herman-Edelstein et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2015; and Rampanelli et al., 2018.

claim: Lipid overabundance can lead to 'lipotoxicity,' which is a main driver of kidney disease progression.
source: Lipid overabundance, however, can lead to 'lipotoxicity,' which is a main driver of kidney disease progression (Abbate et al., 2006; Bobulescu, 2010; Moorhead et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abbate et al., 2006; Bobulescu, 2010; and Moorhead et al., 1982.

claim: In DKD, albuminuria combined with dyslipidemia leads to a tubular overload of albumin-bound fatty acids.
source: This is particularly true in DKD, where albuminuria combined with dyslipidemia leads to a tubular overload of albumin-bound fatty acids (Bonventre, 2012; Zeni et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bonventre, 2012 and Zeni et al., 2017.

claim: Within cells, lipid overabundance leads to enhanced triacylglycerol (TAG) synthesis and lipid droplet (LD) formation.
source: Within cells, lipid overabundance leads to enhanced triacylglycerol (TAG) synthesis and lipid droplet (LD) formation.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular lipid metabolism that draws from established knowledge.

claim: TAG synthesis occurs at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where three fatty acids are consecutively added via esterification to the glycerol backbone beginning with sn-glycerol-3-phosphate.
source: This process occurs at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where three fatty acids are consecutively added via esterification to the glycerol backbone beginning with sn-glycerol-3-phosphate.
evidence: This describes the biochemical process of TAG synthesis, which is established knowledge.

claim: Once enough TAGs (and cholesterol esters) have been deposited between the ER lipid bilayer leaflets, LDs bud into the cytoplasm enwrapped by a phospholipid monolayer.
source: Once enough TAGs (and cholesterol esters) have been deposited between the ER lipid bilayer leaflets, LDs bud into the cytoplasm enwrapped by a phospholipid monolayer (Wilfling et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wilfling et al., 2014.

claim: Free saturated fatty acids can activate pro-inflammatory pathways.
source: However, as free fatty acids (in particular, saturated ones) can activate pro-inflammatory pathways (Shi et al., 2006) or generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon excessive mitochondrial ß-oxidation (Gehrmann et al., 2015), storing fatty acids in LDs could also prevent damage (Listenberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2006.

claim: Free saturated fatty acids can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon excessive mitochondrial ß-oxidation.
source: However, as free fatty acids (in particular, saturated ones) can activate pro-inflammatory pathways (Shi et al., 2006) or generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon excessive mitochondrial ß-oxidation (Gehrmann et al., 2015), storing fatty acids in LDs could also prevent damage (Listenberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gehrmann et al., 2015.

claim: Storing fatty acids in LDs could prevent damage.
source: However, as free fatty acids (in particular, saturated ones) can activate pro-inflammatory pathways (Shi et al., 2006) or generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon excessive mitochondrial ß-oxidation (Gehrmann et al., 2015), storing fatty acids in LDs could also prevent damage (Listenberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Listenberger et al., 2003.

claim: LDs can sequester polyunsaturated acyl chains, protecting them from the oxidative chain reactions that generate toxic peroxidated species and ferroptosis.
source: Accordingly, it has been shown in neural stem cells that LDs can sequester polyunsaturated acyl chains, protecting them from the oxidative chain reactions that generate toxic peroxidated species and ferroptosis (Bailey et al., 2015; Dierge et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bailey et al., 2015 and Dierge et al., 2021.

claim: Sequestering free fatty acids by LDs has been shown to protect mitochondrial function during starvation-induced autophagy.
source: Similarly, sequestering free fatty acids by LDs has been shown to protect mitochondrial function during starvation-induced autophagy (Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2017.

claim: In the context of DKD, there is only limited knowledge of the role of TAG and LD formation.
source: In the context of DKD, however, there is only limited knowledge of the role of TAG and LD formation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The butter diet caused more tubular damage and renal fibrosis than the olive oil diet in hyperglycemic mice.
source: While the butter diet caused more tubular damage and renal fibrosis than the olive oil, less lipid accumulation was observed in the renal proximal tubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's mouse experiments, supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Less lipid accumulation was observed in the renal proximal tubules with the butter diet compared to the olive oil diet.
source: While the butter diet caused more tubular damage and renal fibrosis than the olive oil, less lipid accumulation was observed in the renal proximal tubules.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's mouse experiments, supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The tubular damage was more pronounced in PTCs showing less LDs.
source: The tubular damage was more pronounced in PTCs showing less LDs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's histological analysis.

claim: PA induced rapid cytotoxicity by increasing the relative proportion of disaturated TAG precursors in cellular membranes.
source: On a wider level, the integration of lipidomic, transcriptomic, and functional studies revealed that PA induced rapid cytotoxicity by increasing the relative proportion of disaturated TAG precursors in cellular membranes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's integrated multi-omics analysis.

claim: PA-induced cytotoxicity leads to ER stress.
source: This leads to ER stress, which can be fully suppressed by co-incubating with OA.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's functional experiments.

claim: PA-induced ER stress can be fully suppressed by co-incubating with OA.
source: This leads to ER stress, which can be fully suppressed by co-incubating with OA.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's functional experiments.

claim: The protective effect of OA is tightly connected with the formation of unsaturated phospholipids and the formation of LD.
source: This protective effect is tightly connected with the formation of unsaturated phospholipids and the formation of LD that serve as a lipid reservoir to protect against lipid bilayer stress in the ER.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's mechanistic investigations.

claim: LDs serve as a lipid reservoir to protect against lipid bilayer stress in the ER.
source: This protective effect is tightly connected with the formation of unsaturated phospholipids and the formation of LD that serve as a lipid reservoir to protect against lipid bilayer stress in the ER.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's mechanistic investigations.

claim: Nonfasting hyperglycemia became apparent 4 weeks after STZ injection.
source: Nonfasting hyperglycemia became apparent 4 weeks after STZ injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: STZ-injected mice presented polyphagia and polydipsia as a sign of increased glucosuria.
source: In addition, STZ-injected mice presented polyphagia and polydipsia as a sign of increased glucosuria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C and Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C and Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: STZ-injected mice showed increased levels of albumin in the urine.
source: In addition, they showed increased levels of albumin in the urine (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: All three STZ-injected groups showed impaired weight gain over the entire experiment compared to vehicle-injected mice.
source: All three STZ-injected groups showed impaired weight gain over the entire experiment compared to vehicle-injected mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All STZ-injected mice had an extreme loss of epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT), with some mice losing all their eWAT.
source: All STZ-injected mice had an extreme loss of epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT), with some mice losing all their eWAT (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Plasma TAGs levels were increased in diabetic mice fed with MUFA-HFD and SFA-HFD.
source: Concomitantly, plasma TAGs levels were increased in diabetic mice fed with MUFA-HFD and SFA-HFD (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Liver weight was only increased in mice fed with the two HFDs while all diabetic groups showed increased kidney weight.
source: Liver weight was only increased in mice fed with the two HFDs while all diabetic groups showed increased kidney weight (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Diabetic mice on both HFDs massively accumulated LDs in the kidney cortex.
source: Diabetic mice on both HFDs massively accumulated LDs in the kidney cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: In the MUFA-HFD group, the percentage of kidney cortex stained with ORO was higher than in the SFA-HFD group.
source: In the MUFA-HFD group, the percentage of kidney cortex stained with ORO was higher than in the SFA-HFD group.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Individual LDs could be seen in tubules but not in glomeruli.
source: Individual LDs could be seen in tubules but not in glomeruli (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 1D–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Lipid accumulation was particularly evident in PTCs of the straight S2 or S3 segments but not of the convoluted S1 segment.
source: Lipid accumulation was particularly evident in PTCs of the straight S2 or S3 segments but not of the convoluted S1 segment (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: At 12 weeks after the STZ injection, LCN2 levels were higher in mice fed with SFA-HFD than in mice fed with MUFA-HFD.
source: At 12 weeks after the STZ injection, LCN2 levels were higher in mice fed with SFA-HFD than in mice fed with MUFA-HFD (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Only in the mice fed SFA-HFD the increase in fibrotic area reached statistical significance.
source: The staining revealed fibrotic areas in all diabetic mice groups, but only in the mice fed SFA-HFD this increase reached statistical significance (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: When normalized to fat deposition, the increase in the fibrotic area became even more apparent in SFA-HFD kidneys compared to MUFA-HFD kidneys.
source: Moreover, when normalized to fat deposition, the increase in the fibrotic area became even more apparent in SFA-HFD kidneys compared to MUFA-HFD kidneys (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Increased mRNA levels of the profibrotic molecules Ccl5 and Fn1 in SFA-HFD kidneys supported the histological findings.
source: Increased mRNA levels of the profibrotic molecules Ccl5 and Fn1 in SFA-HFD kidneys supported the histological findings (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Strong apical KIM-1 expression was found in renal proximal tubules in some of the STZ and SFA-HFD mice while only moderate in MUFA-HFD kidneys.
source: We found strong apical KIM-1 expression in renal proximal tubules in some of the STZ and SFA-HFD mice while only moderate in MUFA-HFD kidneys (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: None of the concentrations of BSA induced any cytotoxicity in iRECs.
source: However, none of the concentrations of BSA induced any cytotoxicity as measured by the uptake of Cytotox dye using the IncuCyte Live-Cell analysis system (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PA treatment induced cell death after 8 hr in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: PA treatment induced cell death after 8 hr in a concentration-dependent manner, while cell viability was unaffected by OA, even after treatments of up to 7 days (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cell viability was unaffected by OA, even after treatments of up to 7 days.
source: PA treatment induced cell death after 8 hr in a concentration-dependent manner, while cell viability was unaffected by OA, even after treatments of up to 7 days (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both PA and OA effects were independent from the level of confluency.
source: Both PA and OA effects were independent from the level of confluency (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Co-treatment with OA completely rescued the cytotoxic effects of PA.
source: Importantly, co-treatment with OA completely rescued the cytotoxic effects of PA.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Even when only 0.25 mM OA was co-incubated with 0.5 mM PA, cell viability was fully restored.
source: Even when only 0.25 mM OA was co-incubated with 0.5 mM PA, cell viability was fully restored (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Increasing glucose levels mildly enhanced the cytotoxic effects of PA, but this was not statistically significant.
source: Increasing glucose levels mildly enhanced the cytotoxic effects of PA, but this was not statistically significant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In both murine primary PT cultures and OK cells, comparable effects on cell viability were observed when exposed to different doses of albumin fatty acids.
source: In both cell models, comparable effects on cell viability were observed when exposed to different doses of albumin fatty acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The transcriptional response observed in BSA-PA and BSA-OA cells was much more pronounced than in BSA-PA/OA-treated cells.
source: The differential expression analysis showed that the transcriptional response observed in BSA-PA and BSA-OA cells was much more pronounced than in BSA-PA/OA-treated cells (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: Cluster 1, which included genes upregulated by PA and normalized by OA co-treatment, proved to be strongly enriched in genes involved in oxidative stress, ER stress, and autophagy.
source: Cluster 1, which included genes upregulated by PA and normalized by OA co-treatment, proved to be strongly enriched in genes involved in oxidative stress, ER stress, and autophagy (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Important lipid metabolism genes such as the mitochondrial fatty acid importer Cpt1 and the fatty acid desaturases Scd1 and Scd2 belonged to the top-regulated genes.
source: Important lipid metabolism genes such as the mitochondrial fatty acid importer Cpt1 and the fatty acid desaturases Scd1 and Scd2 also belonged to the top-regulated genes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cluster 4, featured by genes that were downregulated by PA and normalized by OA co-treatment, showed a clear enrichment of biological processes controlling cell proliferation.
source: By contrast, cluster 4, featured by genes that were downregulated by PA and normalized by OA co-treatment, showed a clear enrichment of biological processes controlling cell proliferation (Figure 2I), confirming the observation that BSA-PA treatment slows down cell growth compared to the other three conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 2I and cell growth data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Several of the identified TFs whose activities were upregulated by PA and downregulated by OA have known roles in lipid metabolism (e.g., HNF4A, SREBF1) and ER stress (e.g., ATF4, ATF6).
source: Interestingly, several of the identified TFs whose activities were upregulated by PA and downregulated by OA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) have known roles in lipid metabolism (e.g., HNF4A, SREBF1) and ER stress (e.g., ATF4, ATF6).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor activity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and draws from established knowledge about TF functions.

claim: Several TFs whose activities were regulated in the opposite way function in cell cycle control (e.g., E2F4, MYC, FOXM1).
source: By contrast, several TFs whose activities were regulated in the opposite way function in cell cycle control (e.g., E2F4, MYC, FOXM1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor activity analysis and draws from established knowledge about TF functions.

claim: Superoxide levels were increased by PA treatment in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Superoxide levels were increased by PA treatment in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: When OA was added together with PA, the DHE staining returned to basal levels.
source: When OA was added together with PA, the DHE staining returned to basal levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: PA was found to increase mitochondrial activity while OA reduced it.
source: Using tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester (TMRE), which is an indicator of mitochondrial membrane polarization, PA was found to increase mitochondrial activity while OA reduced it.
evidence: This claim is supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: The combination of PA with OA returned mitochondrial activity to basal levels.
source: The combination of PA with OA returned mitochondrial activity to basal levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: Etomoxir treatment increased the PA-induced cytotoxicity.
source: Etomoxir treatment increased the PA-induced cytotoxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: OA was still protective in the presence of etomoxir.
source: However, OA was still protective in this condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: All three ER stress response pathways are activated by PA after 16 hr.
source: qPCR-based ER stress marker analysis of spliced Xbp1 (sXbp1), Hspa5 (also known as Bip), and Ddit3 (also known as Chop) mRNA showed that all three ER stress response pathways are activated by PA after 16 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Full suppression of ER stress activation was achieved by cotreatment with OA.
source: Full suppression of ER stress activation was achieved by cotreatment with OA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The PERK inhibitor slightly reduced the cytotoxicity caused by PA, suggesting that the PERK-eif2a-ATF4 axis may contribute to the cell death process.
source: On the one hand, the PERK inhibitor slightly reduced the cytotoxicity caused by PA, suggesting that the PERK-eif2a-ATF4 axis may contribute to the cell death process.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 3B and involves inference about the mechanism.

claim: The inhibition of IRE1α kinase and RNase activities exacerbated the PA cytotoxicity, arguing for a protective role of IRE1α in response to PA.
source: On the other hand, the inhibition of IRE1α kinase and RNase activities exacerbated the PA cytotoxicity, arguing for a protective role of IRE1α in response to PA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 3B and involves inference about the mechanism.

claim: The SCD1 inhibitor exposed the ER stress responses and enhanced the cytotoxicity induced by low-dose PA.
source: The inhibitor exposed the ER stress responses and enhanced the cytotoxicity induced by low-dose PA, indicating that fatty acid desaturation is critical for preventing PA-induced ER stress (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Fatty acid desaturation is critical for preventing PA-induced ER stress.
source: The inhibitor exposed the ER stress responses and enhanced the cytotoxicity induced by low-dose PA, indicating that fatty acid desaturation is critical for preventing PA-induced ER stress (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 3C and D and involves inference.

claim: Etomoxir exacerbated the ER stress response induced by PA, suggesting that decreased mitochondrial β-oxidation might increase the burden of PA in the ER.
source: Importantly, etomoxir exacerbated the ER stress response induced by PA, suggesting that decreased mitochondrial β-oxidation might increase the burden of PA in the ER (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and involves inference.

claim: OA treatment did not show any protective effect against the ER stress caused by tunicamycin and thapsigargin.
source: Here, OA treatment did not show any protective effect against the ER stress caused by tunicamycin and thapsigargin (Figure 3E), suggesting that the protective effects of OA are specific for PA-induced ER lipid bilayer stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The protective effects of OA are specific for PA-induced ER lipid bilayer stress.
source: Here, OA treatment did not show any protective effect against the ER stress caused by tunicamycin and thapsigargin (Figure 3E), suggesting that the protective effects of OA are specific for PA-induced ER lipid bilayer stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and involves inference.

claim: PA treatment mildly induced the formation of LC3 puncta as well as large perinuclear structures positive for p62, all of which were cleared by the addition of OA.
source: PA treatment mildly induced the formation of LC3 puncta as well as large perinuclear structures positive for p62, all of which were cleared by the addition of OA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: While there was no significant change in LC3I/II levels between BSA and BSA-PA-treated cells, p62 was clearly increased in BSA-PA-treated cells.
source: While there was no significant change in LC3I/II levels between BSA and BSA-PA-treated cells, p62 was clearly increased in BSA-PA-treated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The addition of the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 caused an increase in LC3I/II and an additional increase in p62, which was stronger in PA-treated cells vs. control.
source: The addition of the lysosomal inhibitor bafilomycin A1 caused an increase in LC3I/II and an additional increase in p62, which was stronger in PA-treated cells vs. control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The accumulation of p62 occurs in the presence of normal autophagic flux, possibly because the amount of misfolded proteins due to ER stress exceeds the autophagic clearance capacity.
source: This suggests that the accumulation of p62 occurs in the presence of normal autophagic flux, possibly because the amount of misfolded proteins due to ER stress exceeds the autophagic clearance capacity.
evidence: This claim involves inference from the immunoblotting data.

claim: PA treatment decreased ER membrane fluidity (as evidenced by increased GP values) whereas OA increased it.
source: PA treatment decreased ER membrane fluidity (as evidenced by increased GP values) whereas OA increased it.
evidence: This claim is supported by C-Laurdan imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The addition of OA to PA restored the GP values to normal levels.
source: The addition of OA to PA restored the GP values (Figure 4A and B) to normal levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by C-Laurdan imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Higher membrane order is associated with the PA-induced ER stress.
source: Thus, these results suggest that higher membrane order is associated with the PA-induced ER stress and that the mechanism by which OA suppresses ER stress involves restoring ER membrane order to homeostatic levels.
evidence: This claim involves inference from the C-Laurdan imaging data.

claim: The mechanism by which OA suppresses ER stress involves restoring ER membrane order to homeostatic levels.
source: Thus, these results suggest that higher membrane order is associated with the PA-induced ER stress and that the mechanism by which OA suppresses ER stress involves restoring ER membrane order to homeostatic levels.
evidence: This claim involves inference from the C-Laurdan imaging data.

claim: All four treatments did not differ much in the relative amount and degree of saturation of the major glycerophosholipid species.
source: All four treatments did not differ much in the relative amount and degree of saturation of the major glycerophosholipid species (phosphatidylcholines, phosphatidylethanolamines, phosphatidylserines, phosphatidylglycerols, and phosphatidylinositols).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: While OA treatment led to the strong formation of TAGs, PA-treated cells presented increased levels of precursors of TAGs synthesis, such as diacylglycerols (DAG), phosphatidic acid (PhA), and lysophosphatidic acid (LPA).
source: However, while OA treatment led to the strong formation of TAGs, PA-treated cells presented increased levels of precursors of TAGs synthesis, such as diacylglycerols (DAG), phosphatidic acid (PhA), and lysophosphatidic acid (LPA).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: The addition of OA to PA enhanced the formation of TAGs, thereby reducing the accumulation of DAG, PhA, and LPA.
source: The addition of OA to PA enhanced the formation of TAGs, thereby reducing the accumulation of DAG, PhA, and LPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: PA treatment dramatically increased the saturation index of DAG, PhA, and LPA, and this was fully reverted by OA co-treatment.
source: Moreover, PA treatment dramatically increased the saturation index of DAG, PhA (Figure 5E and F), and LPA, and, again, this was fully reverted by OA co-treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: OA decreased the concentration of free fatty acids, most likely as a consequence of the stimulated TAG synthesis.
source: OA also decreased the concentration of free fatty acids (Figure 5G), most likely as a consequence of the stimulated TAG synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by free fatty acid measurement data shown in Figure 5G and involves inference.

claim: PA treatment caused a general increase in lysophospholipid levels that was accompanied by the transcriptional down- and upregulation of Lpcat1 and Lpcat3, respectively.
source: Additionally, we observed a general increase in lysophospholipid levels (lysophosphatidylcholines, lysophosphatidylethanolamines, lysophosphatidylserines, etc.) by PA that was accompanied by the transcriptional down- and upregulation Lpcat1 and Lpcat3, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics and transcriptomics data.

claim: The downregulation of LPCAT1 likely reflects an attempt to dampen the production of oversaturated phosphatidylcholine species and, thereby, the lipid stress in the ER membrane.
source: The downregulation of LPCAT1 therefore likely reflects an attempt to dampen the production of oversaturated phosphatidylcholine species and, thereby, the lipid stress in the ER membrane.
evidence: This claim involves inference from the lipidomics and transcriptomics data and draws from established knowledge about LPCAT1 function.

claim: OA treatment (0.25 mM) resulted in both higher number and higher size of LDs compared to PA (0.25 mM).
source: OA treatment (0,25 mM) resulted in both higher number and higher size of LDs compared to PA (0.25 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by BODIPY staining data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Combined treatment (PA 0.25 mM + OA 0.125 mM) resulted in LDs smaller in size compared to OA alone.
source: Combined treatment (PA 0.25 mM + OA 0.125 mM) resulted in LDs smaller in size compared to OA alone (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by BODIPY staining data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: The SCD1 inhibition blocked the formation of LDs in PA-treated cells, resulting in LD numbers and sizes comparable to the BSA group.

evidence: This claim is supported by BODIPY staining data shown in Figure 6A, D and E.

claim: SCD1 (possibly together with SCD2) is required for the conversion of PA into MUFAs and subsequent LD formation.
source: Accordingly, the SCD1 inhibition blocked the formation of LDs in PA-treated cells, resulting in LD numbers and sizes comparable to the BSA group (Figure 6A, D and E), suggesting that this enzyme (possibly together with SCD2) is required for the conversion of PA into MUFAs and subsequent LD formation.

claim: When incubated only with BSA, the BODIPY-C12 dye was located in LDs but also in perinuclear membranes that co-localized with the ER marker calnexin.

claim: The combination of DGAT1 and DGAT2 inhibitors completely inhibited the formation of LDs.

claim: In iRECs treated with BSA or PA/OA, DGAT1/2 inhibitors caused only minimal changes in the relative amount and saturation of each lipid class.

claim: In iRECs treated with PA, the DGAT inhibitors caused major disturbances including a massive accumulation of oversaturated TAG precursors (LPA, PhA, and DAG), as well as increased relative levels of saturated lysophospholipids.

claim: A drastic decrease in cholesterol esters was observed in all conditions treated with DGAT inhibitors, suggesting that TAG formation influences cholesterol esterification.
source: A drastic decrease in cholesterol esters was also observed in all conditions treated with DGAT inhibitors, suggesting that TAG formation influences cholesterol esterification (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 7A–C and involves inference.

claim: PA-induced cytotoxicity was strongly exacerbated by DGAT inhibition.

evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: ROS and ER stress markers were increased upon DGAT inhibition.
source: Accordingly, ROS and ER stress markers were increased upon DGAT inhibition (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROS measurement and qPCR data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: The protective effect of OA concerning cytotoxicity and ER stress was unaltered in the presence of the DGAT inhibitors.
source: Interestingly, the protective effect of OA concerning cytotoxicity and ER stress was unaltered in the presence of the DGAT inhibitors, suggesting that OA co-treatment can balance the saturation level of ER phospholipids even if TAG formation is blocked.

claim: OA co-treatment can balance the saturation level of ER phospholipids even if TAG formation is blocked.

claim: OA co-treatment can reduce disaturated DAG levels (especially DAG 16:0_16:0 and DAG 16:0_18:0) and the ratio between disaturated and monounsaturated DAG compared to PA alone no matter if DGATs are inhibited or not.

claim: Pretreatment with OA reduced PA-mediated cytotoxicity.

claim: Treatment with atglistatin in normal and starved conditions caused an increase in cell area occupied by LDs.

claim: ATGL inhibition caused a significant increase in PA-induced cytotoxicity when compared to untreated cells.

evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: LDs serve as a reservoir of MUFAs that can be released via lipolysis to buffer an overload of SFAs.
source: Our results, therefore, suggest that LDs serve as a reservoir of MUFAs that can be released via lipolysis to buffer an overload of SFAs.
evidence: This claim involves inference from the ATGL inhibition data.

claim: MUFAs released from LDs could facilitate the incorporation of SFAs into TAGs or decrease the packing density of ER membrane.
source: MUFAs released from LDs could then facilitate the incorporation of SFAs into TAGs or decrease the packing density of ER membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism by which MUFAs from LDs protect against SFA toxicity.

claim: The diet enriched in MUFA stimulated the synthesis of TAGs while the diet enriched in SFA increased the saturation levels of the DAG species and impaired TAG synthesis in the kidney cortex of STZ-injected mice.
source: In agreement with the histological LD profile of the kidney cortex in these different conditions, the diet enriched in MUFA stimulated the synthesis of TAGs while the diet enriched in SFA increased the saturation levels of the DAG species and impaired TAG synthesis (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data from mouse kidney cortex shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In both STZ-HFD groups, the vast majority of the LD-positive tubules were not marked by the KIM-1 antibody.
source: Interestingly, in both STZ-HFD groups, the vast majority of the LD-positive tubules were not marked by the KIM-1 antibody.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: In the SFA-HFD mice there were more tubules than in MUFA-HFD mice showing increased KIM-1 expression and these were mostly devoid of LDs.
source: As reported above, in the SFA-HFD mice there were more tubules than in MUFA-HFD mice showing increased KIM-1 expression and these were mostly devoid of LDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: In the MUFA-HFD mice there were more LD-positive cells that in turn were mostly KIM-1-negative.

claim: Tubular damage is mainly occurring in the LD-poor tubules.

claim: KIM-1 immunoreactivity was seen in cortical PTCs positive for megalin and SGLT2, while the corticomedullary junction was mostly devoid of KIM-1.
source: KIM-1 immunoreactivity was seen in cortical PTCs positive for megalin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and SGLT2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), while the corticomedullary junction was mostly devoid of KIM-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: KIM-1 expression was also observed in severely damaged tubules that showed partial loss of the segment markers.
source: KIM-1 expression was also observed in severely damaged tubules that showed partial loss of the segment markers (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: One study showed no protective effect of a Mediterranean diet compared to a low-fat control diet with regard to the DKD incidence in type 2 diabetics.
source: While one study showed no protective effect of a Mediterranean diet compared to a low-fat control diet with regard to the DKD incidence in type 2 diabetics (Diaz-Lopez et al., 2015), two studies demonstrated renoprotective effects with adherence to Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) and Mediterranean diets in cohorts of diabetic women (Jayedi et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diaz-Lopez et al., 2015.

claim: Two studies demonstrated renoprotective effects with adherence to Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) and Mediterranean diets in cohorts of diabetic women.
source: While one study showed no protective effect of a Mediterranean diet compared to a low-fat control diet with regard to the DKD incidence in type 2 diabetics (Diaz-Lopez et al., 2015), two studies demonstrated renoprotective effects with adherence to Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) and Mediterranean diets in cohorts of diabetic women (Jayedi et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jayedi et al., 2019 and Yu et al., 2012.

claim: Lipolysis in white adipose tissue might have contributed to renal fat accumulation in addition to increased dietary fat intake.
source: This suggests that, in addition to increased dietary fat intake, lipolysis in white adipose tissue might have contributed to renal fat accumulation.
evidence: This claim involves inference from the observed depletion of white adipose tissue and increased circulating lipids.

claim: The activity of the main albumin receptor cubilin is known to be restricted to the S1 segment.
source: As the activity of the main albumin receptor cubilin is known to be restricted to the S1 segment (Christensen et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2020), other uptake pathways may account for lipid uptake in S2/S3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Christensen et al., 2021 and Ren et al., 2020.

claim: The expression analysis showed strong downregulation of both CD36 and FATP2 genes in all three mice groups treated with STZ compared to the control group.
source: As seen in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, our expression analysis showed strong downregulation of both genes in all three mice groups treated with STZ compared to the control group, which may argue against an important role for them in DKD.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: It was recently shown that the scavenger receptor KIM-1 mediates apical albumin-PA uptake in PTCs to promote DKD.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mori et al., 2021.

claim: It is known that PTCs in the straight segments contain less mitochondria.
source: Indeed, it is known that PTCs in the straight segments contain less mitochondria (Hall et al., 2021; Maunsbach, 1966), possibly resulting in LD build-up due to decreased β-oxidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2021 and Maunsbach, 1966.

claim: Restricted expression of SCD1 to the straight S2/S3 segments could explain the lipid deposition pattern.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2006 and involves speculation.

claim: The inhibition of GPAT enzymes that catalyze the first addition of fatty acids to the glycerol backbone is a promising approach for preventing lipotoxic cell injury.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Piccolis et al., 2019.

claim: DAGs have been implicated in insulin resistance due to their role in activating protein kinase C (PKC) isoforms.
source: For diabetic kidneys, this might be particularly important as DAGs have been implicated in insulin resistance due to their role in activating protein kinase C (PKC) isoforms (Lyu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lyu et al., 2020.

claim: Studies have shown that disaturated DAGs causing ER stress likely involves PERK and IRE1-induced sensing of membrane lipid saturation.
source: How disaturated DAGs cause ER stress is not fully understood, but studies have shown that this likely involves PERK and IRE1-induced sensing of membrane lipid saturation (Halbleib et al., 2017; Volmer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Halbleib et al., 2017 and Volmer et al., 2013.

claim: The altered ER membrane environment may lead to the misfolding of transmembrane proteins and subsequent induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: Additionally, the altered ER membrane environment may lead to the misfolding of transmembrane proteins and subsequent induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential mechanism.

claim: In cell culture and in the mouse kidneys, LD formation correlates positively with the protective effects of MUFAs and negatively with cell damage.
source: Both in cell culture and in the mouse kidneys, LD formation correlates positively with the protective effects of MUFAs and negatively with cell damage.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from both cell culture and mouse experiments.

claim: LD formation was shown to be dispensable for OA-mediated rescue effects in PA-induced stress because OA can reduce disaturated DAGs even in the presence of DGAT inhibitors.
source: Yet, LD formation was also shown to be dispensable for OA-mediated rescue effects in PA-induced stress because OA can reduce disaturated DAGs even in the presence of DGAT inhibitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by lipidomics data showing OA can reduce disaturated DAGs even with DGAT inhibition.

claim: Only when cells were pretreated with OA, then OA-mediated rescue effects were DGAT-dependent.
source: Only when cells were pretreated with OA, then OA-mediated rescue effects were DGAT-dependent, suggesting that the preexistence of LDs is relevant for these rescue effects and/or that the beneficial effects of LD formation lag behind those associated with the formation of unsaturated phospholipids.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data from the OA pretreatment experiment.

claim: ATGL-mediated lipolysis is required for the OA rescue effect.
source: As we also show that ATGL-mediated lipolysis is required for the OA rescue effect, our interpretation is that LDs can function as a reservoir for unsaturated lipids that can be released, for example, when the ER membrane desaturation is increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytotoxicity assay data with ATGL inhibition.

claim: LDs can function as a reservoir for unsaturated lipids that can be released when the ER membrane desaturation is increased.
source: As we also show that ATGL-mediated lipolysis is required for the OA rescue effect, our interpretation is that LDs can function as a reservoir for unsaturated lipids that can be released, for example, when the ER membrane desaturation is increased.
evidence: This claim involves interpretation and inference from the ATGL inhibition data.

claim: Mice exposed to HFD show a striking lipid accumulation pattern with more LDs in the straight S2/S3 PTCs.
source: We find that mice exposed to HFD show a striking lipid accumulation pattern with more LDs in the straight S2/S3 PTCs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the mouse experiments.

claim: MUFA-HFD that leads to more LDs is associated with less injury while the opposite is true for SFA-HFD.
source: Accordingly, MUFA-HFD that leads to more LDs is associated with less injury while the opposite is true for SFA-HFD.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the mouse experiments.

claim: ER membrane saturation is a key determinant of cell viability that is regulated by LDs as a reservoir for MUFAs.
source: Mechanistically, we identify ER membrane saturation as a key determinant of cell viability that is regulated by LDs as a reservoir for MUFAs.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic findings from the study.
